questions.explanation: Some candidates chose C, QR only, because they read a horizontal line as constant acceleration. QR is flat, so the speed is constant and the acceleration is zero. Acceleration on a speed–time graph is the gradient, and the question asks for a gradient that is constant and not zero. That is any straight sloping section: PQ going up and RS going down (a constant deceleration still counts as constant acceleration). ST is curved, so its gradient keeps changing. Answer: B. Before you pick, write the gradient of each section next to the letters.

Some candidates chose B, between 10 kJ and 20 kJ. The report suggested they found only the kinetic energy at the bottom of the hill. Check it: ½ × 80 × 202 = 16 000 J, which sits in that band. The question asks for the energy wasted, which is the energy the cyclist started with minus the energy they finish with. Gravitational potential energy lost = 80 × 9.8 × 50 = 39 200 J. Subtract the 16 000 J of kinetic energy and 23 200 J is left, so C. Wasted energy is always a difference, so work out both ends.

Some candidates chose A, believing the particles in a liquid are further apart and move faster than those in a gas. It is the other way round on both counts. In the liquid the particles are close together. In the gas they are far apart, and heating the liquid to above its boiling point has raised their average speed. So the liquid has the smaller spacing and the smaller average speed: D. Heating a substance increases particle speed and spacing together, so the hotter gas is the one that is faster and further apart.

Most candidates remembered that pressure falls as the volume of a gas at constant temperature rises. Some then picked A, a straight line with a negative gradient, because they treated pressure and volume as linearly related. They are inversely proportional: pV is constant, so doubling V halves p. That gives a curve that falls steeply at small V, flattens at large V and never touches either axis, which is C. A straight line would reach p = 0 at a finite volume, and a gas cannot do that. For any p–V graph at constant temperature, look for the hyperbola.

The report says candidates misread the graph and took a value straight off the horizontal axis as the wavelength. The axis is time, so what you can read from it is the period. The curve crosses zero at 0, 4.0 and 8.0 s, so one complete wave takes 8.0 s. Then use v = fλ, or λ = v × T: 2.0 m/s × 8.0 s = 16 m, which is D. Option C, 8.0 m, is the period with the wrong unit attached. Check the label on the horizontal axis first. If it says time, you must multiply by the speed to reach a distance.

The report found that the wrong answers were spread across A, B and C, which suggests many candidates guessed. Do not guess here; this one is two facts. A short-sighted eye focuses light from a distant object too soon, so the image forms in front of the retina. To push the image back onto the retina the light has to be spread out before it enters the eye, which needs a diverging lens. Answer: D. Learn it as a pair: short-sighted means image in front, correct with diverging.

Some candidates chose B, which has a higher pressure and the particles closer together. That is the description of a compression. A rarefaction is where the particles are spread out, so the average distance D is greater than d and the pressure P is lower than p. Answer: C. Remember the two together: more space between the particles means fewer collisions with the walls and less pressure.

Some candidates chose B, which shows evenly spaced circles. They believed the strength of the field around a current-carrying wire does not change with distance. It does: the field is strongest next to the wire and weakens as you move away, so the field lines are closer together near the wire and further apart outside. That rules out B and D. For the direction, point your right thumb along the current. With the current into the page, the fingers curl clockwise, so the arrows on the left of the wire point up. Only A has both the widening spacing and clockwise arrows.

Incorrect answers were spread across A, B and D, which suggests many candidates guessed. Use the left-hand rule. The field points down the page, from N to S. The electrons travel to the right, so the conventional current is to the left. Point the first finger down for the field, the second finger left for the current, and the thumb points out of the page: C. The usual slip is to use the direction the electrons move as the current. A negative charge reverses the direction you would give a positive one.

Some candidates chose A, 0.30 A, because they believed that if the number of turns falls by a factor of 5 the current falls by a factor of 5 as well. The coils behave in opposite ways. This transformer is step-down: 900 turns on the secondary against 4500 on the primary, so the secondary voltage is 240 × 900 / 4500 = 48 V, and the secondary current is five times bigger. A 100% efficient transformer has equal power in and out: 1.5 × 240 = 360 W, and 360 / 48 = 7.5 A. Answer: B. When the voltage is stepped down, the current is stepped up by the same factor.

Most candidates correctly subtracted the background count from the 200 counts per minute first. Some then made the common slip of adding it back after 8.0 days. Work in three steps. The count due to the source is 200 − 20 = 180 counts per minute. One half-life later, that count is 90. The question asks for the count rate due to the source, so you stop there: B. Option D, 110, is 90 + 20, the reading the detector would show. Read the last line of the question to see which of the two numbers it wants.

Many candidates chose D, believing a lead apron works by reflecting radiation. It does not. The lead absorbs some of the radiation, so less of it reaches the radiographer. That is shielding: C. The other options are the other two ways of reducing exposure, distance and time, and the apron does neither. Know all three safety measures and match the apron to shielding.

Many candidates converted light-years into metres correctly. Some did not then convert the distance from metres into kilometres. One light-year is about 9.46 × 10<sup>15</sup> m, so 4.3 light-years is about 4.07 × 10<sup>16</sup> m. Divide by 1000 to get kilometres: 4.1 × 10<sup>13</sup> km, which is B. Option D, 4.1 × 10<sup>16</sup>, is the figure in metres with km written after it. The question asks for kilometres, so check the unit in the last line and finish the conversion.
